description: Flan, Ouisa, Kitty, Larkin, and Dr. Fine walked quickly through Harvard Yard, their pace urgent, their path cutting directly across the campus grounds.
related_events: FLAN, OUISA, KITTY, LARKIN, and DR. FINE walk urgently through Harvard Yard

name: Geoffrey Promises Extra Funds for Cezanne Sale, Flan Reacts in Shock
description: Geoffrey sits in the back seat of a limousine, speaking on a cordless phone. He tells the person on the line that he has been thinking and that the Japanese buyers really want the Cezanne. He promises an additional overcall of two hundred and fifty thousand dollars. At the same time, Flan stands in the Kittredge's living room and hears the amount. His face shows clear shock at the figure.

Flan reacts with shock to financial figure

description: The wedding guests waved goodbye to Flan and Ouisa as they made their way to their car. The bride and groom stood nearby, present but not the focus of attention. Flan and Ouisa got into their vehicle and drove out of the parking lot.

Flan and Ouisa drive away from the parking lot
related_occasions: Bride And Groom'S Wedding

name: Ouisa and Flan Introduce Themselves to a Detective, Mentioning Harvard
description: Ouisa, Flan, Kitty, and Larkin walk up to a detective who is seated at a desk. They lean in slightly, as if beginning a private conversation. Ouisa speaks first, saying that their two children and the detective’s son are at Harvard together. At this, Kitty and Larkin smile, clearly pleased by the coincidence.

Kitty and Larkin express pleasure about Harvard connection

description: Tess arrives in New York and goes to her mother Ouisa. She takes a small tape recorder from her belt and places it on the desk. She tells Ouisa that she went to MIT and confronted someone in his computer room, pressing him until he spoke. Tess turns the recorder on. Ouisa hears Trent's voice from the tape saying, 'Yes, I knew Paul.'

TESS presents a taped recording to her mother
Ouisa listens to a taped conversation about Paul

name: Dr. Fine Arrives and Identifies Himself
description: Dr. Fine, a man in his 50s, walks down the hall and opens the door to his office. Inside, Flan, Ouisa, Kitty, and Larkin are seated and waiting. He steps in, closes the door behind him, and tells them he was seeing a patient. He adds that he is an obstetrician at New York Hospital.

Dr. Fine explains his role as an obstetrician

name: Paul's Vocal Performance and Response
description: Paul, a young Black man, stands in a room with a white wall and faces the camera. He delivers a sequence of greetings—serious, flirtatious, questioning, suspicious, then elated—each colored with a distinct emotional tone. After his final 'Hello!', a person off screen claps. Paul acknowledges the sound by bowing toward the off-screen presence.

Paul bows to an off-screen presence

description: The detective's phone rang, and he listened quietly before nodding to himself. At the Morgan Library, the string quartet played the final, swelling notes of their piece, filling the room with sound. In the midst of the music, Flan turned and said, 'And a new character entered our story.'

String quartet performs a climactic passage at the Morgan Library
New character is introduced into the narrative

description: The four kids flip through their high school yearbook when Tess points to a photo. They all lean in to look. It's Trent Conway. His picture shows a weasel-faced boy with a distant expression, not quite meeting the camera's gaze. Doug wrinkles his nose, muttering about Trent's beady eyes staring out at him. Woody glances at the others and says, 'He's at MIT now.'

description: Flan and Ouisa, dressed in formal attire, join their friends at a small champagne bar outside the opera boxes. The group stands together, sipping drinks and chatting before the performance. Flan mentions that they all went to Harvard. Ouisa adds that they once had to enlist their children, and the conversation lingers on memories from the past as the others listen.

Flan mentions shared Harvard alumni background
Ouisa recalls enlisting their children

name: Ouisa and Flan Greet Kitty and Larkin
description: As Flan and Ouisa's car approaches the garage, Ouisa leans out the window and waves at Kitty and Larkin, who are crossing the street. Flan honks the horn. Kitty and Larkin glance at the car with a frown, but their expressions shift to smiles when they recognize the couple. Ouisa calls out, 'Do we have a story to tell you!' Kitty immediately responds, 'Do we have a story to tell you!'
related_events: Flan honks horn while approaching garage
Ouisa waves from car window at Kitty and Larkin
Kitty and Larkin react to car with glare then smile

name: Paul and the Unseen Man's Verbal Game
description: Rain falls outside, mingling with the sound of jazz and distant thunder. Paul stands with a bottle of beer in hand. He says, 'Bottle of beer.' The unseen young man, off camera, repeats the phrase with elegant phrasing. Paul responds, 'Bottle—of beer.' The man acknowledges, 'Very good. You owe me.' Paul says nothing, then removes his shirt. He is strongly built. Without hesitation, he throws the shirt directly into the camera.

Paul and unseen man exchange remarks about owing money

description: Paul takes off his shirt, revealing his strongly built body, and throws the shirt directly into the camera.
related_events: Paul removes his shirt and throws it at the camera

Flan objects to Geoffrey's plan to make the call

name: Geoffrey Walks Through the Airport Terminal
description: Geoffrey moves through the airport terminal, his footsteps echoing against the tiled floor as he passes gates and travelers, making his way through the bustling terminal.

description: Geoffrey places his phone on the security conveyor belt. The device moves along the belt and passes through the X-ray scanner. A security officer watches the screen as the phone appears in the scan. Once it exits the machine, Geoffrey picks it up from the end of the belt.

Flan's voice is heard speaking from elsewhere. Geoffrey picks up the phone as it emerges and says his plane is being called. name: Ouisa and Flan Flee Their Apartment
description: Ouisa and Flan run out of their apartment building, their clothes hastily put on, their faces swollen with shock. They hurry down the side street toward the garage where their Mercedes waits. Flan slips a bill to the attendant before getting into the driver's seat. Ouisa takes the passenger seat. Flan says he is shaking. Ouisa offers to drive, but Flan insists he has to hang on. They prepare to leave.
related_events: Ouisa and Flan rush out of their apartment building in distress

description: Ouisa and Flan run down the side street into the garage, their clothes hastily put on, faces swollen with shock. They approach their waiting Mercedes. Flan slips a bill to the attendant and moves to the driver's side. He gets into the car, his hands shaking. Ouisa gets into the passenger seat. 'I'm shaking,' Flan says. 'Then I'll drive,' Ouisa replies. 'I have to hang on,' Flan answers. 'Let's just get there,' Ouisa says.

name: Flan Projects Paintings and Reflects on Lost Art
description: Flan sits at a slide carousel in a vast, bright space and projects images of paintings into the air. As the slides appear, his voice fills the space, speaking about how a painter can work on a canvas for months and then suddenly lose the painting—not just misplace it, but lose its structure, its sense of form and meaning. The projections float and fade as he speaks, suspended in the emptiness around him.

Flan reflects on the loss of artistic structure in painting

name: Teacher Hangs Children's Drawings and Pink Shapes in the Air
description: A bright white light shines as the teacher appears, hanging vividly colored children's drawings in the air. Flan watches and speaks in awe of her second-grade students, calling them artistic geniuses and comparing them to Matisse. He asks why his child’s class is so exceptional and begs to be taken in as a student. The teacher replies that she has no secret, then turns and hangs pink paper shapes resembling a button-down shirt on a long clothesline that stretches into the distance. The shapes float in the air, filling the space with pink.
related_events: Teacher hangs colorful children's drawings in the air

name: The Screen Fills with Pink
description: The screen becomes entirely filled with the color pink. Pink shapes, resembling a button-down shirt, hang in the air like paper on a clothesline that stretches into the distance. The vast space, once empty, is now transformed by the color, which spreads until it dominates the entire visual field.
related_events: Screen fills with the color pink

name: Ouisa Sees Paul in the Dream
description: Ouisa lies awake in the master bedroom while Flan sleeps beside her. In the dim light, a man in dinner clothes sits at the edge of the bed, his back to the room. He speaks to her in a calm, comforting voice, saying he wants to make a movie of Cats not because of the musical’s value, but because life should be about more than just its beginning and end. He talks of the weight of debates over birth and death, and how the long stretch in between deserves attention. As he speaks, Ouisa watches, transfixed. The man turns, and she sees his face clearly—it is Paul. The moment passes, and the figure is gone. Ouisa is asleep. The bed is empty.
related_events: Flan sleeps while Ouisa remains awake in the master bedroom
Ouisa experiences a dream about Sidney Poitier
Sidney Poitier apparition explains motivation for making Cats movie

name: Flan Dreams of Paintings
description: Flan lies asleep in the master bedroom, his face still in the quiet dark. Over his sleeping form, images of paintings by Matisse, Picasso, De Kooning, and Pollock appear, drifting across his features. In his dream, he feels close to the paintings, not as objects to be sold, but as things he once loved. He remembers why he was drawn to art in the first place, what first drew him into the world of paintings, and in the dream, he does not merely sell them—he sees them, feels them, recalls them.
related_events: Flan reflects on his dream about art and his passion for paintings

name: Geoffrey Arrives at the Lounge with a Film Festival Idea
description: Geoffrey walks into the first class lounge, speaking on the radio phone without pause. His driver follows behind, taking care of the luggage. As he moves through the space, Geoffrey continues his conversation, suggesting a black American film festival in South Africa. He mentions Spike Lee as a current figure of interest, proposes Sidney Poitier as president of the jury, and brings up Bill Cosby and Eddie Murphy as people he admires. He also notes that his wife once went fishing in Norway with Diana Ross and her new Norwegian husband.

Geoffrey's driver handles baggage at the airport

name: Flan and Ouisa React to Geoffrey's Proposal

name: Parents Confront Woody in Harvard Building
description: Inside the Harvard building, Doug, Tess, and Ben confront Woody with rising intensity. Doug says Woody never does anything for him. Tess accuses Woody of trying to block her at every turn. Ben declares he’s only become a pathetic extension of Woody’s eighth-rate personality. Doug brings up social Darwinism, saying it’s been taken too far, and reacts when Woody mentions drugs, clearly feeling targeted. Tess tells Woody he wants her to be everything he wasn’t. Amid the chaos, Woody interrupts, demanding to know who gave away his pink shirt. The argument overwhelms the space. One by one, the parents fall silent, then exit the building and walk out onto the street, stunned and defeated. Passersby stop to stare, but Woody doesn’t respond. Pages of a yearbook turn, then stop on a photo of Trent Conway.

Tess confronts Woody about blocking her ambitions
Ben denounces being reduced to Woody's inadequate extension

name: Parents Flee Harvard Building After Woody's Outburst
description: Woody's shouting drives Ouisa, Flan, and the other parents out of the Harvard building and onto the street. They walk away in silence, heads down, not speaking to one another, as passersby pause to watch. The group moves together but without connection, each lost in their own stillness.

Parents walk down street in silence after confrontation

Flan and Ouisa report that there has been no news and that everything has been quiet. They express relief. The group leaves the opera box and heads to the champagne bar. Everyone is in high spirits. Ouisa announces they will be going to Rome. Connie hands Ouisa a card with a name on it. Ouisa reads it and passes it to Flan. Flan smiles, says he has always wanted to meet them, and promises to call as soon as they arrive in Rome. They all laugh and enjoy the moment.

description: Ouisa stirs awake when she hears a tapping at the window. She sits up in bed, looking around the darkened room. Outside, on the ledge, Paul appears in a pink shirt. She gets out of bed and walks to the window, opening it. Paul stands on the other side, now able to speak to her.

description: Paul stands on the window ledge outside the bedroom, wearing a pink shirt. He delivers a quiet, intense monologue about the imagination, speaking of fear, desire, and the voice within. Mid-sentence, he pulls out a switch blade, flips it open, and lifts his shirt. Without hesitation, he stabs himself in the torso. Ouisa cries out in shock and horror as Paul topples backward off the ledge and disappears into the darkness below. The phone rings, breaking the silence, and Flan reaches over to answer it. Ouisa remains seated on the bed, wide-eyed and trembling, the room now still except for the sound of the phone.

Flan reaches for the phone and answers it. Around her, the familiar walls and furniture settle into view—nothing is out of place. The window is closed, the room still. Ouisa exhales, her body relaxing as the weight of the moment passes.

name: The Break-In at Mortimer's Restaurant
description: At Mortimer's Restaurant, Flan and Ouisa meet with Kitty and Larkin for dinner. Kitty and Larkin recount what happened the previous night. In the middle of the night, they heard someone shouting 'Burglar! Burglar!' They rushed into the hallway and saw Paul chasing a naked blonde thief down the corridor. The thief ran out of the building, the alarm went off, and nothing was later found to be missing. Paul stayed calm afterward, and they gave him twenty-five dollars to help until his father arrived. Flan and Ouisa listen closely, asking if anything had been taken and whether they had spoken to their children, but Kitty says she can't get through. The group decides to return to Flan and Ouisa's place.

name: Doug Takes a Late-Night Call from His Father
description: Doug is awakened in his college dorm room by a ringing phone. He reaches under the covers and answers it. His father, Dr. Fine, is on the line. In the examining room, Dr. Fine begins speaking, responding to what he perceives as accusations from his son—that he is uninterested in Doug’s life, a poor friend, and a bad father. Doug interrupts, confused, asking who his father is talking about. He grows angry, calling his father a cretin for giving house keys to a stranger who mentioned Doug’s name at the office. Doug shouts that he is embarrassed to be his son, then brings up painful family history: his mother left, she claimed Dr. Fine beat her, called him a bad lover, said he smelled of cheap wine, and compared being with him to eating a salad with bad dressing. He yells that he wishes he had never been born. A girl in the bed beside him sits up, frightened, then pulls pillows over her head. Dr. Fine continues, insisting there are two sides to every story, but Doug cuts him off, shouting that he is an idiot. In his office, Flan, Ouisa, Kitty, and Larkin listen intently, leaning forward. She considers how Paul found them, how he appeared out of nowhere, like Columbus or Magellan setting sail into unknown waters. name: Ouisa and Flan Arrive at the Wedding
description: Cars are parked outside a wooden chapel near Millbrook, New York. The bride steps out of a limo, escorted by her father. Ouisa and Flan approach her, kiss her on the cheek, and offer cheerful greetings. Ouisa exclaims that the bride looks horrible, then quickly corrects herself, saying she meant the bride looks radiant. Flan adds that they could have been killed. The father asks what happened, but Flan dismisses the comment, calling it a wonderful wedding and a wonderful day. The three hurry into the chapel, where a string quartet plays Dvořák’s American Quartet. An usher in morning clothes greets them and asks which side they are seated on. Flan says he can’t remember how they met the couple. They walk down the aisle with their heads down, kneel, and whisper fragments of a childhood prayer. The couple in front turns around—Sandy and Connie, who resemble Ouisa and Flan but seem more nautical, as if they’ve arrived from Nantucket. Sandy asks if anything is wrong. Ouisa says they were almost murdered. Flan adds that their throats were slashed. The people in front gasp. The quartet begins playing the Wedding March. Everyone stands as the bride and her father walk down the aisle. Inside Ouisa’s mind, vivid colors flash—later revealed to be a Kandinsky painting in her living room. She whispers, “Chaos,” then “Control,” as the image shifts between bright and dark geometric patterns. Back in the chapel, the ceremony ends. The bride and groom run up the aisle, smiling, but slow when they see Ouisa and Flan’s expression. Flan snaps out of it and forces a smile, saying they always get this way at weddings. The couple resumes their exit. Ouisa, still stricken, says she doesn’t always feel this way. Flan reminds her they are alive. They walk up the aisle into the foyer. She rests her head on his shoulder and says it was awful. As they pass through the receiving line, they smile and shake hands with the bride and groom. The bride asks if they really could have been killed. Ouisa says yes, only hours ago. Flan adds that they’re here now. Ouisa says they wouldn’t have missed it. The bride and groom exchange a look as Ouisa and Flan move on.

name: The Children Confront Their Parents in the Dining Hall
description: After lunch, the five parents sit across from their children at the refectory table in the Dining Commons. Students come and go around them. Flan speaks in a hushed tone, suggesting the mysterious boy they encountered must be someone from their high school, possibly gay or involved in drugs. Doug interrupts sharply, his voice echoing, and refuses to hear more. Tess retorts that it could just as easily have been a girl, and resents the assumption that it must involve a gay classmate. She mocks her parents’ taste in theater, pointing out their disdain for Cats and Starlight Express. Ouisa insists they contact everyone from their high school class to find the boy. Doug slams his chair back and demands why his father looks at him when talking about drug users, accusing them of suspecting him of being an addict or dealer. Dr. Fine tells him to sit down, but Doug remains standing. Larkin rises and paces, repeating, 'I don't want to know,' over and over. Flan insists no one is being accused, only asking the kids to investigate. Ben recalls the boy promised them roles in Cats. Ouisa says it was fun, but Tess reminds her she once called such shows a disgrace to Aeschylus. Ouisa denies saying it, and Flan suggests it was Starlight Express instead. Tess snaps back that maybe they’ll all get roles in a movie version on roller skates. The children stand. Doug calls the situation humiliating, Ben says it’s pathetic, and Tess calls it racist. Ouisa insists it’s not. The children walk out into the corridor. The parents rush ahead and block the main entrance. Kitty tells Doug he can’t have outgrown his high school friends already. Ouisa pulls a red book from her bag as the group faces off.

name: Geoffrey's Visit and the Weight of Commitment
description: Geoffrey arrives at Flan and Ouisa's apartment, where they are preparing for an evening at home. Geoffrey responds that someone must stay to educate Black workers, and that they will know they’ve succeeded when those they’ve taught kill them. Flan calls it planning the revolution that will destroy him. Ouisa strokes her dog and says it feels wrong to talk of revolution from their East Side living room, imagining instead that if they visited, they would demand to see the poorest in the townships, seeking real suffering. She jokes about building barricades and singing revolutionary songs. Flan compares her to Gorbachev encouraging coal miners, then sings a line from 'The Fantasticks.' Ouisa mentions China, and both Flan and Ouisa react with despair. Geoffrey says, 'Oy vay China,' as his grandmother would, and speaks of offering themselves to their role in history. Flan insists that such a role belongs to Geoffrey, not to them. Ouisa reflects on the ease with which he claims a role in history. name: Paul Recounts His Father's Early Life
description: Paul leans against the wall, speaking animatedly to someone off camera. He tells the story of his father, Sidney Poitier, who was born on February 24 in Miami while his parents were visiting from the Bahamas, where they farmed tomatoes. His father grew up on Cat Island, in deep poverty—so poor, Paul says, that they didn’t even own the dirt they walked on. Neglected by his family, the boy would sit on the shore, staring out to sea, imagining different worlds and what he would do if he lived in them. At fifteen and a half, he arrived in New York City in the winter of 1943. He slept in the pay toilet of a bus station across from the old Madison Square Garden at Fiftieth and Eighth Avenue, then later moved to the roof of the Brill Building on Tin Pan Alley. He worked washing dishes at the Turf restaurant for $4.11 a night and taught himself to read by studying the newspaper. In the Black newspaper, the theater page was opposite the Want Ads, a detail Paul remembers. His father went on to appear in 42 films, including No Way Out (1950), Cry the Beloved Country (1952), Blackboard Jungle (1955), The Defiant Ones (1958), Raisin in the Sun (1961), Lilies of the Field, In the Heat of the Night (1967), To Sir With Love (1967), and Shoot to Kill (1988). He won an Oscar for Lilies of the Field and was twice named the top male box-office star in the country. He made no films between 1987 and 1988, instead working as a director and author. Paul recalls his father once saying, "I still don't fully understand how all that came about in the sequence it came about." Off camera, someone applauds. Paul laughs, bows, and kicks his shoe off toward the camera.
